note.explanation: Plants remove extra gases, water, and other metabolic wastes in different ways. They release gases through their surfaces and stomata, remove extra water by transpiration or guttation, and get rid of other wastes by storing them or excreting them through special pores.
examples: At night, plants release excess carbon dioxide through their general surfaces and stomata.
Rubber plants excrete latex; keekar trees excrete gums.
note.checkAnswer: Plants remove extra water by transpiration during the day and, in some plants, by guttation at night.
note.simple: Plants cannot move away from wastes, so they release, store, or shed them.
note.checkQuestion: Name the process by which some plants release water droplets through pores at leaf tips or edges at night.
note.title: How Plants Excrete Wastes
steps: Identify the waste: gas, extra water, or another metabolic waste.
For excess gases, state that plants release them through general surfaces and stomata.
For extra water, distinguish daytime transpiration from night-time guttation.
For other wastes, describe storage, removal with fallen leaves, or excretion through special pores.
Give the correct plant example when asked.

mcqs.stem: Which process removes extra water from plants during the day?
rationales: This is correct: plants remove extra water by transpiration during the day.
Guttation is described as a way some plants remove excess water at night.
Dew forms when water vapour in the air condenses on leaf surfaces; it is not plant excretion.
Resin is an example of another metabolic waste, not the process for removing extra water during the day.

written.text: Describe the process of gaseous exchange in plants
written.finalAnswer: During the day, plants use the carbon dioxide produced in cellular respiration for photosynthesis, and the oxygen produced during photosynthesis is used for cellular respiration. Excess oxygen is released into the atmosphere through stomata. At night, when photosynthesis is not occurring, excess carbon dioxide is released through general surfaces and stomata.

written.text: Describe the mechanisms/adaptations in plants for excretion of wastes.
written.finalAnswer: Plants release excess carbon dioxide through general surfaces and stomata, and excess oxygen through stomata. They remove extra water by daytime transpiration and, in some plants, night-time guttation. Other wastes may be stored as harmless crystals or in leaves that later fall, or excreted through special pores by applying force. Examples are latex from rubber plants, gums from Acacia (keekar) trees, resins from coniferous trees, and mucilage from ladyfinger.

example.question: How do plants remove extra water, and how is guttation different from dew?
example.answer: Plants remove extra water by transpiration during the day and, in some plants, by guttation at night. Guttation releases droplets through leaf pores; dew forms by condensation of water vapour in the air on leaf surfaces.

explain.title: Excess gases
explain.body: During the day, plants use the carbon dioxide produced in cellular respiration for photosynthesis. At night, when photosynthesis is not occurring, excess carbon dioxide is released through the general surfaces and stomata. Excess oxygen from photosynthesis is released into the atmosphere through the stomata.

explain.title: Extra water
explain.body: Plants store water in cell vacuoles, which creates turgor and supports soft parts of the plant. If there is extra water, plants remove it in two ways. During the day, plants remove their extra water by transpiration. The three types are stomatal transpiration, cuticular transpiration, and lenticular transpiration.

explain.title: Guttation is not dew
explain.body: Some plants, such as grasses, release excess water at night as droplets through small pores at leaf tips or edges; this is guttation. Dew means the water drops on leaf surfaces formed by the condensation of water vapours present in the air.

explain.title: Other metabolic wastes
explain.body: Some plants store wastes as harmless crystals or keep wastes in their leaves; when the leaves fall, the plant body also gets rid of the wastes. Other plants excrete wastes through special pores by applying force. Rubber plants excrete latexes, Acacia (keekar) trees excrete gums, coniferous trees excrete resins, and ladyfinger excretes mucilage.

mistakes: Do not call dew guttation: guttation is water released by the plant through leaf pores, while dew forms by condensation of water vapour in the air.
Do not say that guttation occurs during the day; the section describes it as a way some plants remove excess water at night.
Do not mix up the plant-waste pairs: rubber—latex, keekar—gums, coniferous trees—resins, and ladyfinger—mucilage.
Do not leave out the release route when describing gaseous excretion: name general surfaces and stomata for excess carbon dioxide, and stomata for excess oxygen.
